title: Public housing: 1.5 million homes in 12 years
detail: Spend 1% of GDP a year (about €17 billion) on public rental homes (*parque público de vivienda*). The money would go to building, to the state's right to buy first when homes are sold (*tanteo y retracto*), to empty homes, to building more homes on the same land and to taking homes from owners. The goal is 1.5 million public homes in 12 years (125,000 a year), with public rents of no more than €600 a month.
c: In our estimate, €17 billion a year is several times what the state spends on housing now. It does not fit the budget plan agreed with the EU without new taxes. 125,000 homes a year is more than the whole country finishes now (100,980 in 2024).

s.t: Housing Ministry: Observatorio de Vivienda y Suelo, annual bulletin 2024 (La Moncloa)

title: Take homes from large company landlords
detail: A law to take homes from private companies step by step: first from owners of more than 1,000 homes, then more than 700, then companies with more than 50 properties. All city buildings and building land of *SAREB* (the "bad bank" created after the 2008 crisis) would go to the state housing company Casa 47.
c: The state can take property only for the public good and with full payment (art. 33 of the Constitution). In our estimate, buying out large owners would cost tens of billions of euros. Choosing owners by their size would be challenged in court as unfair and as against the EU rule on free movement of money.

title: End tourist flats within 3 years
detail: Within 3 years, end all tourist flat licences (*VUT*) and "short-term" rentals (*alquiler de temporada*) that the programme calls fraudulent, in residential buildings in stressed areas. Tourist rentals would pay 21% VAT and up to 150% extra property tax (*IBI*). Any rental of 30 days or less would count as tourist use.
c: The regions and town halls give tourist flat licences. Catalonia strongly limited them (Decreto-ley 3/2023), and the Constitutional Court said this was legal (ruling 64/2025). But the state does not have this power for the whole country.

s.t: Constitutional Court ruling 64/2025: Catalan decree on tourist flats (BOE)

title: Rent limit: 25% of local household income
detail: In stressed areas, the highest rent would be the lower of two numbers: 25% of the average net household income in the neighbourhood (*sección censal*), or the limit from the official state rent price index (*SERPAVI*). The programme expects market rents to fall by 35% on average, and by another 30% in cities with over 200,000 people or a lot of tourism.
c: A strict limit based on local incomes, not on the market, goes further than today's index. Germany's Constitutional Court cancelled Berlin's rent limit in 2021, because the state of Berlin had no power to pass it, and rents just outside the city went up sharply. Studies in Catalonia disagree on whether fewer homes were offered for rent.

s.t: Hahn, Kholodilin, Waltl, Fongoni, Management Science 70 (2024): the Berlin rent freeze
Monras, Montalvo (2023), Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco WP 2023-28: rent control in Catalonia
Jofre-Monseny, Martínez-Mazza, Segú (2023), Universitat de Barcelona: rent control in Catalonia

title: 10% yearly tax on large landlords' homes
detail: A yearly charge of 10% of the value of homes. Companies would pay from their first property, and people from their fourth if the total value is more than €800,000. Homes rented at stable affordable prices would not pay. It also ends the special tax rules for property investment companies (*SOCIMI*).
c: Paying 10% of the value every year could in practice take the property away, so courts could cancel it as a confiscatory tax (art. 31.1 of the Constitution). The likely result is that owners sell and move their money away, not more affordable rentals.

title: Large companies pay at least 20% tax on profits
detail: Large groups of companies would pay at least 20% on their adjusted profit (instead of 15% today). Small businesses (*pymes*) would pay no more. Groups could no longer combine the accounts of their companies to pay less tax, and they could use past losses to lower tax for only 4 years.
c: An EU rule sets a 15% minimum, and higher rates are allowed. Since 2024 large groups in Spain already pay at least 15% (Ley 7/2024). 20% would raise taxes for large groups, but it is realistic only with a majority.
pos: Large companies pay more and have fewer ways to lower their tax.
neg: Spain would be above the OECD global minimum (15%), so profits and investment could move to other countries.

s.t: Directive (EU) 2022/2523 on the global minimum tax (BOE copy of the OJEU)
Ley 7/2024: 15% minimum tax and bank levy for 2024–2026 (BOE)

title: Tax on large fortunes from €1 million
detail: The tax on large fortunes (*Impuesto de Solidaridad de las Grandes Fortunas*) would start at €1 million of net wealth instead of €3 million (the first €700,000 would be tax-free). All fortunes above €1 million would pay at least 2%, with higher rates from €50 million. It would be a state tax, so regional tax cuts could not cancel it.
c: The solidarity tax already exists (from €3 million). In our estimate, starting at €1 million would reach hundreds of thousands of people, mostly through homes and family businesses. Regions with a wealth tax will balance it in their own way.
pos: More tax money from the largest fortunes, and less inequality. Because it is a state tax, regions can no longer bring it down to zero, so there is less tax competition between them.
neg: In our estimate, a tax from €1 million would also reach middle-class owners of an expensive flat in Madrid or Barcelona. It also gives rich people a reason to move their money away.

s.t: Ley 38/2022: solidarity tax on large fortunes, bank and energy levies (BOE)

title: Lower income tax up to €27,000, up to 52% at the top; end the Beckham regime
detail: No income tax (*IRPF*) on the minimum wage, with the tax cut getting smaller up to €27,000 (1.5 times the SMI). New bands from €120,000, and a top rate of 52% from €300,000. Income from savings and investments would pay closer to the rate on wages. End the special regime for foreign workers who move to Spain (*régimen de trabajadores desplazados*, the "Beckham law") and the tax deductions for private pension plans.
c: It is technically simple. The programme does not say if the 52% includes the regional part of income tax. If it does not, the top rate would go above 60% in some regions, one of the highest in the EU.
pos: No income tax on the minimum wage, so more money for people who earn little.
neg: In our estimate, a 52% rate would be one of the highest in Europe. People with high incomes would have a reason to leave or to change how they are paid.

title: Retirement age back to 65
detail: Bring the retirement age (*edad de jubilación*) back to 65 (the 2011 reform raised it). People in hard jobs, such as building, cleaning and fishing, could retire from 60. People who paid social security for more than 40 years would get no cut for retiring early (*coeficientes reductores*).
c: In our estimate, 65 for everyone would cost about 1 to 2% of GDP a year by 2040. It also goes against the pension promises in Spain's EU recovery plan. The age is already 65 for people who paid social security long enough: 38 years and 3 months in 2026, and 38.5 years from 2027.

s.t: Real Decreto Legislativo 8/2015, General Social Security Law (BOE)

title: 37.5-hour week now, 32 hours as the goal
detail: Move at once to 37.5 hours a week, and 35 hours in the public sector, with no loss of pay. Employers could not pay overtime instead of giving time off. Then, step by step, go down to 32 hours a week.
c: 37.5 hours already failed in Congress in 2025, and 32 hours has no chance. The regions decide whether their public workers move to 35 hours.

s.t: Congress, BOCG 15-A-58-3: 37.5-hour bill returned to the government (10 Sep 2025)

title: A permanent way to get legal status
detail: Finish the special regularisation of 2026, change the Immigration Law (*Ley de Extranjería*) and create a permanent, regulated way to get legal status (*regularización*). Appointments at immigration offices within 7 days through a free public booking system.
c: The 2026 regularisation was done by royal decree (RD 316/2026), which changed the immigration regulation. A government that wants a permanent route could make it the same way, without 176 votes. A later government could undo a decree the same way. Changing the Immigration Law itself needs an organic law (176 votes), and PP and Vox are against it. EU law does not ban regularisation, but several EU countries criticise large ones.
pos: Fewer people work without contracts, so the state gets more tax and social security payments, and workers are exploited less.
neg: A permanent route may attract more people to come (experts disagree on how many). It also puts a lot of pressure on offices, as in the 2026 regularisation (1.17 million applications).

s.t: Real Decreto 316/2026 on the 2026 regularisation, changing the immigration regulation (BOE)
La Moncloa, 2 Jul 2026: 1,174,978 regularisation applications filed

title: Fewer obstacles: *padrón*, bank account, diplomas
detail: Easier town-hall registration (*empadronamiento*), a right to a free basic bank account (*cuenta de pago básica*), faster recognition of foreign degrees (*homologación de títulos*), and a duty for companies and offices to accept migrants' documents.
c: An EU rule already guarantees a basic account. Easier registration mostly depends on the town halls.
pos: Migrants settle in faster and can work in jobs that match their qualifications.
neg: More work for town halls. If addresses are not checked, fake registrations become easier.

title: Three hours of free electricity a day
detail: Free electricity for all households during sunny hours, when there is too much power. A public electricity company (*comercializadora pública*) would offer 3 free hours a day, and large companies would have to offer them too. The competition authority CNMC would check that other hours do not get more expensive.
c: Some tariffs already offer free hours. But forcing every company to offer them would be hard to fit with the EU electricity market rules, where the market sets the prices.

title: Close the Almaraz nuclear plant in 2027 to 2028; stop using fossil fuels
detail: Close Almaraz I and II as first planned, with no tax breaks. End state money for fossil fuels, close gas power plants (*ciclos combinados*) by 2045 and ban imports of gas from fracking.
c: In August 2026 the government allowed Almaraz to run until June 2030 (Orden TED/864/2026), so closing it in 2027 or 2028 would mean cancelling the permit. In our estimate, prices could rise and Spain could use more gas. Ending gas by 2045 is realistic.
pos: Less nuclear waste and fewer fossil fuels, and a faster move to clean energy.
neg: Cancelling the 2030 permit would lead to legal fights with the owners. In our estimate the plant produces about 5 to 7% of Spain's electricity. If nothing is ready to replace it, prices and emissions may rise.

s.t: Orden TED/864/2026: Almaraz extended to 8 June 2030 (BOE)
REE, March 2026: the Spanish electricity system in 2025 (renewables 55.5%, nuclear 19%)
